summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under that same system. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

An aggregate index rates the collectivity 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors.
tangentialFactors:
No government travel advice addressing LGBT+ visitors exists for Saint Barthélemy, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office records no warnings for the destination. Absence of official advice is an information gap rather than an assessment of safety.

No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index, so the rating rests on legal and structural data instead of first-hand accounts from trans travellers.

The framework is national, so no local ordinance in Saint Barthélemy narrows or widens the protections a visitor encounters; there is no sub-national variation to account for on the ground.

The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for diverse guests. Discretion is the prevailing norm among a high-end, transient clientele, which keeps any visible scene absent rather than suppressed.

Crime is recorded as low and no hostility toward gay or trans visitors appears in the sources, a context that sits beside rather than offsets the documented detention risk under French prison policy.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether hormone prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment can be filled on Saint Barthélemy itself is not resolved in the sources; only the aggregate index's red flag for limited healthcare access is documented, so the specific local availability of endocrine care remains unverified.

The sources do not describe the collectivity's own detention capacity or the facility in which a person detained here would in fact be held; they establish only that detainees fall under the French prison system and its placement policy.

The methodology and weighting behind the 7.7 out of 10 rating, and how the nine positive rights are scored, are not set out in the material available here.

No source addresses whether offences motivated by gender identity attract sentence enhancement as hate crimes in Saint Barthélemy, so that protection is neither confirmed nor excluded.

No first-hand reports from trans visitors to Saint Barthélemy were available, since no trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the index; the social picture rests on descriptive accounts of the destination rather than traveller testimony.
